vignette: The ambush in the narrow alleyways still played behind Duy’s eyes, a combat deployment that had abruptly ended his childhood. He was eighteen when his unit walked into the crossfire, rifle fire echoing off concrete walls, followed by the wet thud of bodies hitting the ground. He remembered the weight of his rifle, the desperate sweep across the choke point, and the moment the supply runner beside him simply didn’t get up. Duy fired until the magazine ran dry, but the exposed geometry of the street left him helpless. When the fire stopped, only ringing ears and silence remained. In the months that followed, quiet moments at home grew unbearable. Even in his own bedroom, he lay rigid, muscles coiled, unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. Ordinary noises—a car backfiring, a heavy door closing, the click of his camera shutter—made him jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people. He caught himself leaning forward, eyes locked on exits, treating every shadow like a threat. His breath would catch in his throat, muscles locking as if ready to dodge incoming fire. As a photographer, Duy’s days revolved around chasing light through crowded city streets, but the work slowly became a minefield. He would stand near construction sites or busy intersections, waiting for the perfect shot, only for a sudden drop of a metal tool or a distant siren to instantly bring back the full memory without warning. The scene would overwrite reality: cordite would bleed into wet pavement, and crowds would blur into combatants. This suspicion seeped into his work; he stopped collaborating with artists, isolating himself in editing suites where he controlled every variable. The guilt of that day began to calcify into a heavy conviction. He was certain that he should have protected others and he failed, a belief that hardened his heart and made him drift from friends until he no longer felt he belonged anywhere. Because of that core shame, his nervous system refused to stand down, and that unrelenting arousal directly fed his recollections, making the past feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things. The cycle tightened as months passed. Because Duy had come to believe he should have protected others and he failed, his threat state remained locked in survival mode. This conviction amplified every sensory input, and when a loud bang triggered him, the startle response flooded his body with adrenaline, instantly bridging the gap to the past. The memory would surface with visceral heat, carrying a rage on recall so intense it often left him breathless. What frightened him most was how those flooding memories, in turn, hardened his negative beliefs. Each intrusion validated his fear that he no longer belonged anywhere. His hyperarousal became a self-fulfilling prophecy; by constantly scanning for danger, he constructed the isolation he feared. His inability to relax and his habit of taking too many risks or doing things that could cause him harm eroded his relationships, cementing the appraisal that people simply couldn't be trusted. The more he pushed into reckless situations, the more his body stayed locked in survival mode, deepening his conviction that his original failure was a permanent truth. By the time he sat in my office, the photographer now moved through the city like a ghost. His equipment sat untouched, gathering dust because stepping outside felt like walking onto a minefield. He had come to me because quiet moments had finally become impossible. The physical toll of his risk-taking, the constant startle fracturing his sleep, and the way memories ambushed him during daylight had crossed a line. He wasn't looking for a diagnosis; he wanted to lower the alarm bell screaming in his head. He was most afraid that the alleyway’s guilt would never stop dictating his present, but he hoped for a chance to walk a street without feeling like a stranger.
